messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Higher blood vitamin D level was associated with lower depression traits in the UK Biobank cohort.
Sentence: "Our study results suggested that VD was negatively associated with depression and anxiety."
Measured as: depression traits
Population: UK Biobank cohort participants
Intervention: Blood vitamin D level (observational exposure)
Comparator: Lower blood vitamin D levels across participants
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not differ from placebo in seasonal affective symptom scores (SIGH-SAD) at 12 weeks.
Sentence: "There were no significant between-group differences in SIGH-SAD sums at 12 weeks (p = 0.7 (CI: - 3.27 to 4.81))."
Measured as: SIGH-SAD sum
Population: Healthcare professionals with seasonal affective symptoms (SPAQ-SAD question 2 score of 8 or more)
Intervention: 70 μg vitamin D daily for 3 months
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 50
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"A cross-sectional observational association between blood vitamin D and depression traits points one way, while a placebo-controlled supplementation trial found no effect, and the trial's wide CI (-3.27 to 4.81) is only partly informative.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"design_or_bias","also_differs":["population","outcome_measure","intervention"],"detail":"observational cross-sectional (UK Biobank) vs small RCT (n = 50) of 70 μg/day for 12 weeks in seasonal affective symptoms"}
